title: Developing (Learning) Skills - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton describes how skills move through the four visible states of learning and, in addition, through Beginning, Developing and Mastering phases that repeat at every higher level. The new stage is the hardest because the skill looks least like what the learner imagines, which is why many abandon an instrument or activity early unless a coach reframes it. The consolidating stage is the most rewarding, as the learner starts to self-correct and gain confidence. Treading water is the base camp for the next level and conserves brain energy, whereas drowning leads to collapse or opting out. He closes with what skills learning looks like in classrooms: visible struggle, stops and starts, slower pace, shared coaching relationships and judgement-based assessment.
points: Making skills sticky needs repeated experience of three kinds: ample in-class time, practice outside the classroom, and chunking at the learner's level of challenge.
Skills always have a next level, so people should say consolidating, developing and mastering, not consolidated or mastered.
The new stage of skills learning is the most fragile, since it feels like failure, and without coaching and a map of progression many learners give up.
Homework is only helpful once a learner is consolidating, because earlier it extends bad struggle without support.
Treading water gives confidence, a foundation for the next level and relief for limited brain energy.
quotes: The trick to making skills sticky is three-fold. We have to be given repeated experiences, just like knowledge.

We all either find or get shown the level we should be at or we opt to stay at a level because moving onto the next level doesn’t really matter to us. In skills learning, there is always a next level of Beginning, Developing and Mastering, always another process of new, consolidating and treading water in our learning.

There is an obvious reason why so many people give up their instrumental lessons in the early days, the ‘new’ days, of learning. Precisely because it is new, because it is so far from what we imagine or know to be ‘developing’ or ‘mastering’ level playing, it feels like failure.
The better news is that if the New stage of skills learning is the most problematic in all of learning, then the Consolidating stage, providing we are helped to get there, can be the most rewarding.

Consolidating feels so much better than New; our skills performance starts to look like it is supposed to and more like we imagined it would. It’s important that we gain this confidence, important that we feel like this. It will stand us in good stead for the future.

The second, and even more important benefit of treading water for skills learning, is that treading water at one level of our skills development provides the base camp for future levels of each skill. As we move on to the next level, it is the base we have previously laid down that provides the foundation for the good struggle to come rather than a bad one.

Skills learning is a paradox. In almost every area, being able to get better at skills brings advantages and benefits that are academic, technical and personal. But the process of getting better is a tricky one, where struggling is unavoidable and where teachers who are good coaches are essential to making those struggles good ones.
